# Security implications {#security-implications}

Security implications (including “[10-SecurityRequirementsChecklist](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1JUsJl_98OI8p9rXvLlAThqHey0wx_qOp3h2JPtYR3B0/edit)” and “[10-SDLC-SecureCoding](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1JUsJl_98OI8p9rXvLlAThqHey0wx_qOp3h2JPtYR3B0/edit)”) have been considered for this feature and it is determined that there is no risk and no impact.

We met with Security & Operations to discuss any security concerns for Virtual Care programs. The review surfaced the continued use of open text answer fields. Checking with Engineering, Security & Operations was reminded that our coding framework “sanitizes” any data entered into our app before it is injected into the DB (such that any active code entered is eliminated). So our continued use of open text answer fields have no impact on our security posture."

#### Introduction: {#introduction:}

Insomnia is more common than you might think. Over 852 million adults have chronic insomnia worldwide. In the United States, 30% of the population report some insomnia symptoms.

#### What you’ll learn:  {#what-you’ll-learn:}

Practice evidence-based techniques from cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) to improve your sleep quality and overall wellbeing. 

#### 

#### Who is this for: {#who-is-this-for:}

This program is for anyone struggling with symptoms of insomnia.

Education

**Module title:** 

###### Understanding Insomnia {#understanding-insomnia}

**Body:**

Many people struggle to get adequate or restful sleep. Over 40 million people in the United States have chronic insomnia, and over 30% of the population will experience some form of insomnia in their lifetime.

Insomnia is a sleep disorder characterized by trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking up too early, and it results in a poor quality of sleep and daytime impairment.

(headline) Causes of Insomnia  
The causes of insomnia can be a combination of these factors: 

* Psychological factors, such as stress, anxiety and depression  
* Medical conditions, such as chronic pain, sleep apnea, restless leg syndrome or other health issues  
* Lifestyle factors, such as nutrition, physical activity or napping habits  
* Environmental factors, such as noise, light, temperature or an uncomfortable sleep setting

###### Insomnia Severity Index {#insomnia-severity-index}

**Body:**

##### S1M4 {#s1m4}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Sleep Basics {#sleep-basics}

**Body:**

Sleep is a vital biological process that happens in 2 main stages: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep consists of light sleep and deep sleep, during which our bodies grow and heal. REM sleep, the dream stage, is important for memory consolidation and learning.

(headline) The body clock and sleep drive systems  
The circadian rhythm, our internal body clock, works on a 24-hour cycle and helps guide when we feel sleepy or awake. Melatonin, the hormone that regulates our sleep drive, increases as daylight fades, which helps us feel sleepy at night. These 2 systems work together to manage our sleep-wake cycle.

(headline) The benefit of a consistent sleep-wake schedule  
Keeping a regular sleep-wake schedule helps our body clock and sleep drive systems work better. Going to bed and getting up at the same time every day can regulate our body clock and increase melatonin at the right times. Going to bed or waking up just an hour later can affect the body’s internal clock and melatonin production, making insomnia worse. This is why healthy sleep habits, like a consistent sleep-wake schedule, are so important for managing insomnia.

\<button\> Mark as done

**Resource:**  
[Sleep and Your Health](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TeyH7GDxZi-vaLIQ14To2_wyzC0JoKX01X_X36KVF0U/edit#)

##### S1M5 {#s1m5}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Sleep Medications {#sleep-medications}

**Body:**

When people have insomnia or trouble sleeping, they sometimes turn to sleep medications, like prescription drugs or over-the-counter aids. These medications work by interacting with brain chemicals to make you feel sleepy. 

While these medications can help induce sleep, they do not cure underlying sleep disorders. They are typically recommended for short-term use due to their side effects and potential for dependence. Always consult a healthcare provider before starting a new medication.

In addition, research shows the effects of sleep medications may be small. They may only add about 10-30 minutes to your total sleep time and help you fall asleep about 10 minutes quicker. 

Melatonin is sometimes used as a short-term sleep aid. It works by increasing your melatonin levels, which promotes a state of calm wakefulness. Melatonin alone does not cause sleep. Melatonin is not always regulated by government agencies, like the FDA. Discuss with your healthcare provider before taking melatonin.

In 2016, the American College of Physicians began recommending insomnia therapies, like this program, as first-line treatments instead of medication. In many cases, therapeutic interventions are a better long-term solution for insomnia than medications.

##### S1M6 {#s1m6}

**Module type:**  
Reflection

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Why CBT-I? {#why-cbt-i?}

**Body:**

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a short-term, evidence-based psychological treatment. It is designed to improve sleep by changing thoughts and behaviors that interfere with sleep. Many studies and clinical trials show that CBT-I is one of the most effective ways to treat insomnia. 

Throughout this program, you will use CBT-I techniques to address these 6 goals:

1. Build a sleep routine that retrains your brain and body to expect sleep.  
2. Improve sleep quality through sleep consolidation and extension.  
3. Practice strategies to relax your mind and body at bedtime and help you fall asleep.  
4. Analyze your current beliefs and thoughts about sleep, and consider if there are more helpful alternatives.  
5. Learn behavioral strategies to better cope with worries that affect your sleep.  
6. Practice lifestyle habits that are proven to improve sleep.

Let’s start right now. A core aspect of CBT-I is behavioral change, meaning you need to be willing to change the way you do things in order to improve your sleep. Take a moment to consider right now if you are ready and willing to change your habits, thoughts and actions.

\<button\> Reflect

**Question Page:**

* To better enjoy time with friends and loved ones  
* To be more present at work  
* Other

\[Multiple choice, multi-select\]

If other, what are your motivation(s)? (optional)  
\[open answer field\]

##### S2M2 {#s2m2}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### What is Sleep Hygiene? {#what-is-sleep-hygiene?}

**Body:**

A healthy sleep routine begins with proper sleep hygiene, a set of practices that promote good quality sleep and daytime alertness. Studies show that these are the key elements to having effective sleep hygiene:

* Create an environment in your bedroom that promotes sleep.  
* Set and maintain a regular sleep schedule, going to bed and waking up at the same time each day.  
* Spend 30-60 minutes unwinding and relaxing before bed every night.  
* Create a morning routine that promotes daytime alertness in the morning.  
* Avoid taking naps.  
* Avoid stimuli that promote alertness too close to bedtime, including caffeine, alcohol, large meals, phones, TVs, computers and other screens.

In this {{session}}, you will build your sleep hygiene by practicing each of these elements. As you try various sleep hygiene strategies, you will discover what works best for you and build your unique sleep routine. 

\<button\> Mark as done

##### S2M3 {#s2m3}

**Module type:**  
Action

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Optimize Sleep Space {#optimize-sleep-space}

**Body:**

Set the stage for sleep by creating a comfortable and relaxing sleep environment. An optimal sleep space has these qualities:

* Appropriate temperature — the ideal range is 62-68 degrees Fahrenheit.  
* Quiet — try ear plugs and/or a sound machine if noise is an issue for you.  
* Dark — make your room as dark as possible. Consider getting blackout curtains.  
* Screen-free — remove screens from your sleep space as best you can (TV, computer, tablet, etc.). Do not use your phone in bed. If you use a digital clock for an alarm, turn the clock so it faces the wall or cover the screen.  
* Comfortable — what can you do to make your bedroom as comfortable as possible? This could mean reducing clutter or adding things that make you feel relaxed. Consider getting lavender candles or essential oils for added relaxation.

Take time this week to optimize your bedroom for sleep.

##### S2M4 {#s2m4}

**Module type:**  
Care Plan

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Bedtime Routine {#bedtime-routine}

**Body:**

A bedtime routine is a powerful strategy that can help you sleep better. It is a set of activities you do each night to signal to your brain and body it's time for sleep. With practice, this routine can train your internal body clock to expect sleep. Consistency is key — aim to do your routine at the same time every day.

Start your routine 30-60 minutes before you plan to sleep. It's important to make a routine that fits your lifestyle and do it at the same time each night. Your routine might include things like brushing your teeth, changing into your pajamas, washing your face or taking a bath or shower. You could also read a book, do some gentle stretches or relaxing yoga, meditate or write a list of things you're grateful for.

Your routine should not include any screens. The blue light from TVs, phones and tablets blocks melatonin production and release, which can make you feel more awake and make it harder to fall asleep.

Create a bedtime routine and try it a few times this week. Record observations in your sleep log about what helps and what doesn’t, then make adjustments as necessary.

##### S2M5 {#s2m5}

**Module type:**  
Care Plan

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Morning Routine {#morning-routine}

**Body:**

A morning routine also improves your sleep-wake cycle by signaling to your body that it is time to be awake and alert. Create a routine that is unique to you, and practice it at the same time every day. Try it a few times this week. Keep track of what you do and how well it works in your sleep log. In fact, writing in your sleep log can be a part of your morning routine\!

Research shows that the best morning routines include 3 elements:

(headline) 1\. Sunlight

When your eyes and skin experience sunlight in the morning, they signal to the rest of your body that it is time to wake up. This helps set your body clock. Try to get 15-30 minutes of sunlight first thing in the morning. If you can't get natural sunlight, a sun lamp can be a good substitute.

(headline) 2\. Physical movement

Move your body within the first hour of waking. This could be going for a walk, riding your bike or even doing chores like dishes. The goal is to wake up your brain and body with movement. 

(headline) 3\. Personal motivation

Start your day with something inspiring to boost your energy. You could listen to happy music, write a list of goals for the day or chat with someone you care about. 

One thing to avoid in your morning routine is hitting the snooze button on your alarm clock. The extra sleep you get from snoozing doesn't have the same health benefits and can negatively impact your internal body clock. Instead, aim to wake up at a realistic time and try not to hit snooze.

##### S3M2 {#s3m2}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Sleep Consolidation {#sleep-consolidation}

**Body:**

Sleep consolidation is a CBT-I technique designed to improve your sleep efficiency. This means the time you spend in bed sleeping is more productive for you physically and mentally. 

In this technique, you focus on sleep quality rather than quantity by creating a customized sleep schedule. You will initially restrict the time you spend in bed to match the amount of time you actually sleep at night. Then, you gradually increase your sleep window by 15-30 minutes per week. This process is called sleep extension.

For example, you may notice that you tend to go to bed at 10 pm and get out of bed at 7 am, but only sleep for 5 hours a night. You would initially adjust your bedtime and wake time to match that 5 hours of sleep, such as going to bed at midnight and getting up at 5 am. This is the consolidation part of the process. The following week, you might be ready to move your bedtime 15-30 minutes earlier and go to bed at 11:30 pm or 11:45 pm. This is the extension part of the process.

This new sleep schedule means that you will spend fewer hours in bed. You may find it difficult to stay out of bed until your new bedtime. Many people find it helpful to brainstorm activities they can do in the extra “awake time.” For example, some people use this time to tackle household chores or projects they’ve been putting off. Having a list of options already prepared will help you stay out of bed until your new bedtime. 

Sleep consolidation can be challenging in the beginning, because you are setting a strict limit on the amount of time you will spend in bed. However, studies show that this technique can improve sleep quality.

**Audio:**

**Module title:** 

###### Consolidated Bed Time {#consolidated-bed-time}

**Body:**

Take a moment to set your new bed and wake times now:

1. Determine how many hours you typically spend asleep. You can review your sleep logs to help you do this.   
2. Choose a bedtime and wake time that is equal to the number of hours you actually sleep.   
3. Brainstorm what you can do to stay out of bed until your new bedtime.

Follow this sleep schedule for the rest of this {{session}}. If you feel this method may benefit you, continue with sleep consolidation and extension for the rest of the program. Your goal is to gradually increase the amount of sleep you are getting by moving your bed or wake time by 15-30 minutes each week. 

If you do not feel like this method is working for you, you do not have to continue it. You may want to reach out to a sleep specialist for more support. Talking to your healthcare provider is a good place to start.

##### S3M4 {#s3m4}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Stimulus Control {#stimulus-control}

**Body:**

Stimulus control is a CBT-I behavioral technique that helps regulate your sleep-wake cycle. The goal is to retrain your brain and body to associate your bed with sleep. In this technique, you make the following behavioral shifts:

1. Go to bed at night only when you are sleepy.  
2. Get out of bed if you can’t sleep for 15-20 minutes (either when falling asleep or if you wake up).   
3. Get out of bed at the same time each day on weekdays and weekends, regardless of how much sleep you get.   
4. As best you can, reserve your bed and bedroom for sleep and sex only. Do not read, watch television or work in bed, during the day or at night.

Studies show these methods are effective at improving sleep quality. The key is to be consistent and practice these behaviors every day.

##### S4M2 {#s4m2}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Mindfulness and Relaxation Practices {#mindfulness-and-relaxation-practices}

**Body:**

Stress is a common contributing factor to insomnia. When you are stressed, your body releases the hormone cortisol. The function of the hormone is to keep you awake in case you face an imminent physical threat. However, with many modern stressors, it is often more helpful to sleep and approach our challenges with a calm, rested mind. 

(headline) How relaxation and mindfulness help insomnia

Mindfulness and relaxation techniques can help you fall asleep at bedtime or fall back to sleep if you wake up during the night. Mindfulness is the practice of intentionally shifting into the present moment and unhooking from negative thoughts, difficult emotions and past or future stressful situations. Relaxation techniques include breathing exercises, guided imagery and progressive muscle relaxation (or PMR).

##### S4M5 {#s4m5}

**Module type:**  
Action

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Progressive Muscle Relaxation {#progressive-muscle-relaxation}

**Body:**

The stress of daily life can cause your muscles to become tense, making it more difficult to fall asleep at bedtime. Progressive muscle relaxation is a proven technique to release muscle tension and help you relax before bed. Try it tonight.

(headline) Progressive muscle relaxation

1. Spend a moment noticing how different parts of your body feel.  
2. Then, focus your attention on your toes, first on your left side and then on your right. Tighten your toes for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
3. Next, focus on your lower leg muscles. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
4. Then, focus on your upper leg muscles. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
5. Next, focus on your stomach muscles. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
6. Then, focus on your hands. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
7. Next, focus on your lower arm muscles. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
8. Then, focus on your upper arm muscles. Tighten them for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
9. Next, shrug your shoulder muscles for 5 seconds and then relax them on each side.  
10. Finally, close your eyes tightly for 5 seconds and then relax them.

##### S4M6 {#s4m6}

**Module type:**  
Action

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Guided Imagery and Savoring {#guided-imagery-and-savoring}

**Body:**

Guided imagery and savoring are great relaxation techniques to practice when lying in bed waiting for sleep to come. They help your mind slow down and distract you from worrying about sleep. Try at least one of these techniques tonight. 

(headline) Guided imagery

Guided imagery is a cognitive control method where you picture yourself in a relaxing story. Imagine yourself moving through the story. It’s similar to counting sheep, but instead, you are the focus. This method can help you *float* off to sleep instead of *trying* to sleep. Start with one of these prompts or create your own:

* “I’m lying under the warm sun on a sandy beach…”  
* “I’m lying in a hammock on the deck of a lakeside cabin…”  
* “I’m gently strolling through a sleepy village…”

For example: “I’m lying under the warm sun on a sandy beach. I can feel the grainy sand beneath my feet. I can see palm trees swaying in the wind. I can hear the waves crashing on the beach. I can smell the salt in the ocean’s water. Then, I pick up my favorite book and begin to read. I am thirsty, so I take a drink of cool, refreshing water. I am enjoying my book, but the warm sun is making me sleepy. I decide to take a nap.”

(headline) Savoring  
To practice savoring, think of something you enjoy. This could be a specific thing, like a chocolate chip cookie, a memory or an experience you enjoyed. Picture it in your mind, and ask yourself the following questions:

1. “What do I see, hear and smell?”  
2. “How do I feel? Am I happy or proud? Content or relaxed?”  
3. “What other good things or memories does it remind me of?”

##### S5M2 {#s5m2}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Worry and Sleep {#worry-and-sleep}

**Body:**

We all experience worry. When you have insomnia, it is common for your worried thoughts to keep you up at night. By learning about the different types of sleep worries, you can begin to notice your own thought patterns and consider if alternative thoughts would be helpful to you. 

(headline) 3 kinds of sleep worries  
There are 3 common types of worries that keep people up at night:

1. Worries about daily life \- “I made an awkward comment in a meeting. My coworkers must think I’m so dumb.”, “I’m never going to finish my taxes in time.”  
2. Worries about sleep \- “How long will it take me to fall asleep tonight?”, “Will I be able to sleep through the night?”  
3. Worries about how sleep will affect your daily life \- “If I don’t get enough sleep tonight, I won’t be able to function tomorrow.”, “I have an important day tomorrow; I have to get some sleep tonight.”

(headline) How CBT-I can help with sleep worries  
The CBT-I technique of cognitive restructuring teaches you to assess your worried thoughts and consider more balanced, alternative thoughts. This can help you let go of the worries that are keeping you up at night.

(headline) When worry becomes too much  
Excessive worry can be a sign of anxiety. An anxiety disorder is defined as excessive fear or apprehension about real or perceived threats that leads to changes in behavior or physical symptoms. If you find that you are fixating on “what ifs” and "worst-case scenarios,” consider reaching out to your healthcare provider for more support. 

\<button\> Mark as done

---

##### S5M3 {#s5m3}

**Module type:**  
Reflection

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Beliefs about Sleep {#beliefs-about-sleep}

**Body:**

Lack of sleep can sometimes cloud our thinking. For those having trouble sleeping, certain beliefs about sleep might seem true, but may not line up with what science tells us. Consider these common beliefs about sleep and understand the scientific facts behind them. This might make it easier to sleep better.

(headline) “I need at least 8 hours of sleep every night.”  
Though the average population needs 8 hours of sleep, your individual sleep needs may be different. Sleep needs also lessen with age. For individuals with insomnia, sleep quality increases with fewer hours spent in bed. Spending more time in bed than necessary can cause insomnia to worsen. A shorter night of sleep can improve sleep through sleep consolidation.

(headline) “If I can’t sleep, I should just try harder.”  
The brain and body know how to sleep naturally. The harder you try to make yourself sleep, the harder it becomes to actually fall asleep. It is more helpful to focus the mind elsewhere and let sleep come.

(headline) “If I don’t sleep enough, I can’t function.”  
Think about a time when you slept poorly. Though you were likely tired, you were probably able to accomplish most of the things you needed to do. You may not have executed tasks to the best of your ability, but you likely did not have zero ability to function.

(headline) “If I slept poorly last night, I am more likely to sleep poorly tonight.”  
 A bad night of sleep actually increases sleep drive, making it more likely for you to sleep better after. It is common with insomnia to have a bad night or 2 of sleep, followed by a particularly good night of sleep. 

(headline) “If I want to catch up on sleep, I need to go to bed earlier.”  
A regular sleep schedule with consistent bed and wake times can actually help you better. When feeling sleep deprived, build your sleep drive by staying up until the bedtime you have chosen. This way, you will fall asleep faster or fall back asleep more quickly in the night.

\<button\> Reflect

* I need at least 8 hours of sleep every night

* If I want to catch up on sleep, I need to go to bed earlier

\[multiple choice, multi-select\]

##### S5M4 {#s5m4}

**Module type:**  
Evaluate

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Balanced Thoughts {#balanced-thoughts}

**Body:**

When your thoughts and worries are keeping you up at night, a thought record is a CBT-I tool that can help you assess your thoughts and consider more helpful alternative ones. To create a thought record, think of a recent belief or worry about sleep and follow these steps:

1. **Identify the situation** \- Where are you? What are you doing when you think this thought?  
   Example: “I’m lying in bed waiting to fall asleep.”  
2. **Identify the thought** \- Be as specific as you can.  
   Example: “If I don’t fall asleep soon, I will be a wreck tomorrow and have a terrible day at work.”  
3. **Identify the emotion** \- What emotion do you feel when you think this thought?  
   Example: “I feel frustrated, anxious and on edge.”  
4. **Evaluate evidence for and against** \- What evidence or information supports this thought? What disproves it?  
   Example: “Evidence for this thought: I’ve struggled at work in the past when I had a bad night’s sleep.” “Evidence against: when I slept poorly, I still did what I needed to do and made it through the day.”  
5. **Create an alternative thought** \- What is a more balanced thought you could consider instead?  
   Example: “If I sleep poorly tonight, I may have a harder day tomorrow, but I will make it through the day and probably sleep better tomorrow.”

##### S5M5 {#s5m5}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Thinking Traps {#thinking-traps}

**Body:** 

Research shows there are certain types of “thinking traps” we all engage in sometimes. When you are sleep deprived, you are particularly inclined to fall into these thinking traps. Knowing how to identify them will help you recognize when your thinking may be overly negative or distorted.

* **Catastrophizing** – jumping straight to the worst-case scenario when evaluating a situation.  
  **Example:** “If I don’t get a full 8 hours of sleep, my day will be a disaster tomorrow.”

* **All-or-nothing thinking** – seeing things in extreme terms and ignoring the wide spectrum of possibilities between the extremes. This thinking trap is easy to recognize by the presence of the terms “always” or “never.”  
  **Example:** “I can never sleep in beds that are not my own.”, “I always sleep terribly before an important event.” 

* **Personalization** – believing that what others do and say is a direct, personal reaction to something you have said or done.  
  **Example**: “My teammate looks upset. It must be because I didn’t sleep well last night and gave a terrible update about our project at the team meeting this morning.” 

* **Discounting the positive** – overvaluing negative information that supports your negative thoughts and beliefs and devaluing positive and neutral information.  
  **Example**: Fixating on the fact that “I was awake from 2-4 am,” instead of focusing on the restful sleep before and after that.   
    
* **Emotional reasoning** – mistaking feelings for facts. Using your feelings to draw rational conclusions.  
  **Example:** “I feel hopeless that I will ever sleep well again/feel well-rested again, therefore the situation *is hopeless.*”  
    
* **Mind reading** – believing that we know what others are thinking and basing our actions on this assumption.  
  **Example:** “I slept terribly, so everyone must think I look like a wreck.”

\<button\> Mark as done

##### S6M2 {#s6m2}

**Module type:**  
Exercise

**Audio:**

**Module title:** 

###### Worry Time {#worry-time}

**Body:** 

Sometimes people mistake worrying with problem-solving. Worrying is thinking over and over about worst-case scenarios and other bad things that might happen. It doesn't help solve problems, but instead can make you more worried.

Signs you might be worrying include thinking more about what you don't want than what you do want, focusing on past or future problems and feeling physical signs like a fast heartbeat or sweating.

If worries keep you awake at night, try setting aside 10-30 minutes during the day, away from bedtime, to make a stress list. Write down things that stress you out or make you worried or angry. Next to each item, write down things you can do to help address it. Be as detailed as you can. If possible, schedule a time to work on these actions. Start with easier ones. Update your list as you complete items. This should help reduce your worries over time.

\<button\> Complete exercise

**Module title:** 

###### Grounding Technique {#grounding-technique}

**Body:**

This grounding technique is a simple way to shift out of worried thoughts and back into the present moment. Take a moment to try it now. Repeat it any time you notice that you are feeling worried or upset. 

(headline) 5 senses grounding exercise    
This technique directs you to engage with each of your senses as a way to ground yourself in the present moment. This tool is particularly helpful in moments of difficult or strong emotions. Take a moment, shift your attention to your 5 senses and notice:

* 1 thing you can see   
* 1 thing you can smell  
* 1 thing you can feel with your body, like a chair or an itchy sweater   
* 1 thing you can hear  
* 1 thing you can taste, like coffee lingering in your mouth

##### S6M5 {#s6m5}

**Module title:** 

###### Emotional Acceptance {#emotional-acceptance}

**Body:**

Emotional acceptance means understanding your feelings instead of ignoring or trying to change them. Accepting emotions can lead to more peaceful sleep in these ways:

* Lowering stress — understanding your feelings can reduce stress, helping you relax for better sleep.  
* Promoting mindfulness — this helps you focus on now, not past or future worries, aiding sleep.  
* Reducing night worry — accepting feelings means less worry at night, making sleep easier.  
* Managing emotions better — this can prevent strong upsetting feelings from keeping you awake.

Take a moment to watch the video and practice emotional acceptance now.

##### S7M2 {#s7m2}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Nutrition for Sleep {#nutrition-for-sleep}

**Body:**

**Healthy eating improves sleep quantity and quality**. Lack of sleep can also create a hormone imbalance that promotes overeating and weight gain. Studies suggest avoiding eating large meals at least 3 hours before bedtime. This allows enough time for your body to digest the food you ate, but not so much time that you will wake up hungry and disrupt your sleep. 

One study found that a lack of calcium, magnesium and vitamins A, C, D, E and K can contribute to poor sleep. However, some supplements and over supplementation can actually disrupt your sleep. If you think a nutritional deficiency may be affecting your sleep, talk to your healthcare provider about getting tested for nutritional deficiencies and what supplements to take. 

(headline) Build a healthy plate

![][image1]

Image Link: [MyPlateDiagram\_DiabetesPrevention\_005.png](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gjyTgaPVsTFVixuqmt2s-kmF0Mcwad0H/view?usp=drive_link)

A balanced diet that includes a variety of vegetables and fruits can contribute to better sleep. To build a healthy, well-balanced meal, follow this model:

* ½ of your plate should be non-starchy vegetables, such as leafy greens, carrots, onions or tomatoes  
* ¼ of your plate should be whole grains and starchy foods, such as whole wheat bread, black beans, brown rice, corn, lentils and oatmeal  
* ¼ of your plate should be lean protein, such as fish, tofu, lean ground beef, pork loin and chicken and turkey without skin  
* Optional: a small side of fruit, a small amount of low-fat or non-fat dairy, a low-calorie drink

\<button\> Mark as done

**Resources:**

* [MyPlate](https://www.myplate.gov/)   
* [Eat Good to Feel Good](https://www.diabetes.org/healthy-living/recipes-nutrition/eating-well)  
* [Healthy Plates Around the World](https://institute.org/health-care/services/diabetes-care/healthyplates/)

##### S7M3 {#s7m3}

**Module type:**  
Reflection

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Caffeine, Alcohol and Nicotine {#caffeine,-alcohol-and-nicotine}

**Body:**

Drinking caffeine, alcohol or using nicotine close to bedtime can worsen your sleep.

Caffeine stays in your body for a long time. If you drink it at 2 pm, some is still in your body at midnight. Try to avoid caffeine after 2 pm.

Alcohol can make you feel sleepy at first, but it can also wake you up later, shorten your REM sleep and worsen sleep apnea.

Nicotine can reduce your total sleep time too. A study found using nicotine at night can result in 40 minutes less of sleep.

For better sleep, avoid alcohol and nicotine within 4 hours of going to bed.

##### S7M4 {#s7m4}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Naps {#naps}

**Body:**

If you sleep badly, you might want to nap. But if you have insomnia, sleep researchers agree that napping during the day will not help you sleep better at night.

Think of naps like snacks before dinner. Just like a big snack can make you less hungry for dinner, a nap can make you less ready for sleep at night. This is because as the day goes on, your body builds a need for sleep, called “sleep drive”. A nap can reset this sleep drive, making it harder to sleep at night.

If you feel sleepy during the day, instead of napping or drinking coffee, try going outside for a quick walk in the sunlight. It can help you feel more awake and full of energy\!

\<button\> Mark as done

##### S7M5 {#s7m5}

**Module type:**  
Action

**Audio:**  
Yes

**\#required:**  
3

**Tracking content:**  
Log at least 3 days

**Module title:** 

###### Exercise {#exercise}

**Body:**

**Moving your body helps you sleep better.** Research shows that exercise can help decrease insomnia and other sleep issues. 

Moderate exercise each day, just 30 minutes or less, can have a positive impact on your sleep. The most important thing is to do it regularly. Find an activity you like and make it a part of your weekly routine for the best results. 

However, studies also recommend avoiding exercise 3 hours before bedtime. If you exercise within 3 hours of going to bed, your body temperature may not cool down sufficiently, your heart rate might still be high and the stress hormones released during exercise could prevent the release of melatonin. All of these can make it harder to fall asleep, disrupt the quality of your sleep and cause you to wake up more often during the night.

Get more exercise for 3 days. Then, see how this affects your sleep.

##### S7M6 {#s7m6}

**Module type:**  
Reflection

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Stress and Sleep {#stress-and-sleep}

**Body:**

Stress and sleep affect each other. Too much stress can make it hard to sleep, and not enough sleep can make you feel more stressed. Stress can also cause you to worry. Managing stress can help manage the worried thoughts that keep you up.

Cortisol, the stress hormone, plays an important role in the sleep cycle. When cortisol levels are low, melatonin is released, signaling the body to fall asleep. When cortisol levels (stress) are high, you have a reduced ability to fall asleep.

Here are 3 strategies to lower stress:

1. **Organize your tasks**: Pick the 1-3 most important things to do and start there. You can refer back to your worry list for inspiration. If you're short on time, set a time limit. If you have a lot to do, decide what tasks need to be done well and what tasks just need to be done.  
2. **Rest**: Take a short break to relax. Even just 10 minutes can help.  
3. **Get help**: If you're feeling too stressed, ask someone you trust for emotional support or help with tasks.

Think about if stress might be making it hard for you to sleep, and what you could do to feel less stressed.

##### S8M3 {#s8m3}

**Module type:**  
Reflection

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Preventing Relapse {#preventing-relapse}

**Body:**

The skills you have practiced in this program are designed to help you sleep better for the rest of your life. Yet, it is also normal for life’s challenges to cause setbacks. When sleep struggles arise, remember these key strategies:

* Consistency is key; go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.  
* Get out of bed when you can’t sleep.  
* Practice healthy sleep hygiene (no screens, dark room, etc.)  
* Use a thought record to catch unhelpful thoughts and consider more balanced alternative thoughts.  
* Practice emotional acceptance.  
* Use relaxation techniques to calm your mind and body before bed.  
* Resist the urge to nap.  
* Eat healthy, exercise, avoid caffeine after 2 pm and avoid alcohol and nicotine within 4 hours of bedtime.

Reflect on what might trigger a relapse for you and what you can do about it.

* Worrying about the past or future  
* Getting too little exercise  
* Other

##### S8M4 {#s8m4}

**Module type:**  
Education

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### When to Get More Help {#when-to-get-more-help}

**Body:**

Insomnia is often accompanied by other challenges, such as depression, anxiety and chronic pain. If you are continuing to struggle with poor sleep or think any of the health conditions below may apply to you, reach out to your healthcare provider or a sleep specialist for more support. 

(headline) Depression and anxiety  
It is common for people experiencing depression or anxiety to have trouble with sleep. In some cases, addressing depression or anxiety can improve sleep quality and quantity.

(headline) Other sleep disorders  
Sleep disorders affect many people and can have a significant impact on their mental and physical wellbeing. A few other common sleep disorders include:

* **Narcolepsy** is a disorder of daytime sleepiness accompanied by sudden muscle weakness. It is sometimes referred to as daytime sleep attacks.   
* **Restless leg syndrome** is defined by a sensation of cramping, pain or tingling in the legs while trying to sleep.  
* **Sleep apnea** is a common disorder that causes snoring and results in poor sleep quality. Chronic sleep apnea can have long-term negative effects on your heart, lungs and cognition.

(headline) Other health issues  
If you are still struggling with sleep, talk to your healthcare provider. You could be suffering from chronic pain or another health condition that is leading to poor sleep, and this should be addressed immediately. 

\<button\> Mark as done

##### S8M5 {#s8m5}

**Module type:**  
Care Plan

**Audio:**  
Yes

**Module title:** 

###### Personalized Sleep Plan {#personalized-sleep-plan}

**Body:** 

In this program you have practiced the following CBT-I techniques to improve your sleep. Review what worked best for you and create your personalized sleep plan to follow moving forward.

(headline) CBT-I techniques  
**Sleep log** \- track your sleep patterns so you know what methods are working best for you.  
**Sleep space** \- set the stage for sleep by creating a calm, quiet, dark sleep space.  
**Bedtime routine** \- prepare your mind and body for sleep by doing the same routine 30-60 minutes before bed every night.  
**Morning routine** \- get up at the same time each day, move your body and get some sunlight (15-30 minutes).  
**Sleep hygiene** \- only use your bed for sleep, avoid screens 30-60 minutes before bed and get out of bed when you can’t sleep.  
**Sleep consolidation and extension** \- go to bed at a time when you are most likely to fall asleep and gradually extend your sleep window by 15-30 minutes until you reach your goal.  
**Relaxation and mindfulness** \- use relaxation and mindfulness techniques, like 4-7-8 breathing and progressive muscle relaxation, to relax your mind and body after you get in bed.  
**Balanced thinking** \- catch unhelpful thoughts and beliefs. Consider more balanced alternatives.  
**Manage worry** \- notice when you worry about sleep and when your worries keep you awake. Set aside dedicated “worry time” during which you can practice proactive problem solving.  
**Pro-sleep lifestyle** \- eat, exercise and manage stress for better sleep. Avoid napping.

\<button\> Create plan

* No phones, TVs or other screens  
* Comfort
